summary: A proposal to add two File Transfer Protocol commands, ReaDMailFile and ReaDMail, that would let a user read mail stored at a site without logging in. They mirror the existing MLFL and MAIL commands for sending. The authors note that handling users with several IDs is left for later.

eli5.summary: A way to check your mailbox on a faraway computer without logging in, matching the way you already could drop letters in.

questions: how to read mail via ftp
what are rdmf and rdml commands
subtitle: Reading mail through the file transfer protocol without logging in.

tldr.problem: Users stored mail at multiple network sites but had to log in to each one to read it.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 458 proposes two new FTP commands, RDMF and RDML, that let users retrieve mail from a remote server without logging in, mirroring the existing MLFL and MAIL commands used for sending.
tldr.outcome: The proposal enables remote mail access but leaves open the problem of users with multiple network identities.

today: RFC 458 was never widely adopted. The problems it identified—fragmented mail storage and multiple identities—were addressed by other protocols such as SMTP and standards for mail forwarding.

sections.title: The Mail Reading Problem
sections.content:
Early network users stored mail at one or more remote sites but had no simple way to retrieve it. The File Transfer Protocol (FTP) already had commands to send mail: MLFL (mail file) and MAIL (mail). RFC 458 proposes adding symmetric read commands so users could fetch their mail without logging into the remote system.

The RFC identifies a deeper problem: users with multiple network identities and the same identity claimed by different users. The authors note these issues are not yet solved but believe a solution should include a mechanism for all a user's mail to go to a single repository.
sections.eli5: You can send mail to a faraway computer using FTP, but you have to log in to read it. This note says: add commands to read it without logging in.

sections.title: The RDMF and RDML Commands
sections.content:
The proposal defines two commands. RDMF (read mail file) retrieves mail and sends it over the data connection, returning status codes over the control connection. RDML (read mail) returns both mail and replies over the control connection, using a new code 152 to signal that mail text follows.

Both commands handle the case where no mail is waiting by returning the text NO MAIL NOW. Success replies include codes such as 200 or 250. Failures are reported with codes like 433, 450, 451, 454, 455, 457, 500, and 507, with some commands also generating secondary replies.
sections.eli5: The two new commands work like the existing mail-sending commands but in reverse: one sends mail on a separate connection, the other sends it mixed with the status messages.

sections.title: Why This Matters
sections.content:
Network mail was distributed across sites. Without read commands, users either had to log in to multiple hosts (requiring credentials at each) or use different mail protocols at different sites. Symmetric read and write commands in FTP would unify the experience. The RFC notes that a user might even write a program to automatically retrieve mail from all their sites.

FTP's existing password protection mechanism would apply to these new commands, providing security where needed.
sections.eli5: If you can mail a letter to a faraway place, you should be able to check your mailbox there using the same tool, not have to learn a different method.
